title: Floquet Driving of Enzymatic Reactions: Counting Statistics and Long-Time Currents
authors: Yuki Watanabe, Yuki Ishiguro, Takashi Oka
abstract: Technologies for artificially controlling chemical reaction systems, such as optogenetics, are rapidly advancing, making it increasingly important to understand reaction dynamics under time-dependent control. When the modulation of reaction rates is periodic in time, the Floquet formalism provides a systematic framework. We develop a Floquet theory for classical stochastic processes that enables the calculation of the current and its counting statistics under such periodic modulation. In particular, we formulate the theory in terms of a counting field and derive general expressions for the first cumulant and the corresponding current. The current is expressed using the effective Floquet generator and the kicked state, and we further obtain general asymptotic expressions for the current in both the high- and low-frequency regimes. As a concrete example to test our analytical expressions, we then apply the results to discrete Floquet driving -- a non-perturbative, stepwise protocol. The setup is motivated by a biochemical system known as cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) production, which is an enzymatic reaction activated and inhibited by G-proteins. This is formulated as a discretely driven Michaelis--Menten-type reaction model, in which the catalytic activity is switched on and off abruptly in time, and we obtain analytical expressions and numerical results showing how periodic switching of reaction rates generates a long-time product current. In particular, in the high-frequency limit, we show that the effect of the periodic driving can be interpreted through an effective modification of the chemical reaction rates. These results provide a basis for Floquet analysis of periodically driven chemical reactions.
summary: This paper extends Floquet theory to classical stochastic processes to study chemical reaction rates under periodic external driving. By developing a counting field formalism, the authors derive general expressions for the long-time current and its statistics. The results are particularly valuable as they provide non-perturbative insights into how fast or slow modulation affects steady-state chemical output.
main_problem: The paper develops a Floquet theory for classical stochastic processes to analyze reaction dynamics under periodic, time-dependent control.
main_result: It derives general expressions for the long-time product current and its counting statistics, showing that high-frequency driving modifies effective chemical rates.
method: The authors use a counting field formalism applied to the master equation, developing systematic asymptotic expansions (high- and low-frequency) based on Floquet theory.
model_or_system: The model is an enzymatic reaction (Michaelis–Menten type) whose rate constants are periodically modulated. The dynamics are described by a time-dependent master equation recast into a Schrödinger-like form using a counting field.
key_observables: Long-time product current ($J_\infty(\Omega)$), net production ($	ext{NP}(t)$), and the cumulant generating function $S(\chi; t)$.
important_parameters: Driving frequency ($\Omega$), modulation period ($T$), and the high/low-frequency limits of $\Omega$.
main_assumptions: The theory is designed to handle non-perturbative, stepwise switching protocols where smooth approximations fail. Approximations involve systematic expansions in powers of $1/\Omega$ (high frequency).
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically compares continuous vs. discrete/stepwise driving protocols; Figure 7 illustrates the exponential convergence of the calculated current to its long-time steady state.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the counting-field formalism for time-periodic generators, then derives general expressions for $J_\infty(\Omega)$, followed by detailed derivations and asymptotic expansions in both high-frequency (van Vleck) and low-frequency regimes.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful theoretical framework—Floquet analysis combined with counting statistics—to analyze non-equilibrium steady states in open quantum/stochastic systems driven periodically, which is highly relevant to quantum control.
